lessons.title: Roman Numerals
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Roman numerals use letter symbols: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10. A smaller symbol after a bigger one is added (VI = 5 + 1 = 6). A smaller symbol just before a bigger one is subtracted (IX = 10 − 1 = 9).

Worked example: Write the Roman numerals for 2, 5, 12, 16, 7, 9, 19 and 20 (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: Build each number from the symbols I = 1, V = 5, X = 10.
Step 2: 2 = I + I = II.
Step 3: 5 = V.
Step 4: 12 = X + I + I = XII.
Step 5: 16 = X + V + I = XVI.
Step 6: 7 = V + I + I = VII.
Step 7: 9 = X − I = IX.
Step 8: 19 = X + IX = XIX.
Step 9: 20 = X + X = XX.
Answer: 2 = II, 5 = V, 12 = XII, 16 = XVI, 7 = VII, 9 = IX, 19 = XIX, 20 = XX.

Worked example: Count the chocolates and write the number in Roman numerals (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: Count the top row of the picture: 5 chocolates.
Step 2: Count the bottom row: 5 chocolates.
Step 3: Add: 5 + 5 = 10.
Step 4: 10 in Roman numerals is X.
Answer: X (ten chocolates).

Worked example: Count the dice in the pile and write the number in Roman numerals (Exercise 1, Q3)

Step 1: Top layer: 1 die.
Step 2: Middle layer: 2 dice.
Step 3: Bottom layer: 3 dice.
Step 4: Add: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
Step 5: 6 in Roman numerals is VI.
Answer: VI (six dice).

Worked example: Fill in the missing number or Roman numeral: 6, IX, 15, XVII, XX (Exercise 1, Q4)

Step 1: 6 = VI.
Step 2: IX = 9.
Step 3: 15 = XV.
Step 4: XVII = 17.
Step 5: XX = 20.
Answer: 6 = VI, IX = 9, 15 = XV, XVII = 17, XX = 20.

mcqs.q: What number does the Roman symbol V stand for?
mcqs.why: The notes give the three symbols used in this lesson: I = 1, V = 5 and X = 10, so V stands for 5.

mcqs.q: What is VI in ordinary numbers?
mcqs.why: A smaller symbol after a bigger one is added: VI = 5 + 1 = 6.

mcqs.q: What is IX in ordinary numbers?
mcqs.why: A smaller symbol just before a bigger one is subtracted: IX = 10 - 1 = 9.

mcqs.q: How do we write 12 in Roman numerals?
mcqs.why: Build 12 from the symbols: 12 = 10 + 1 + 1, so 12 = X + I + I = XII.

mcqs.q: How do we write 19 in Roman numerals?
mcqs.why: Split 19 into 10 and 9: 19 = 10 + 9, and 9 = IX, so 19 = X + IX = XIX.

mcqs.q: What is XVII in ordinary numbers?
mcqs.why: Add the symbols one by one: XVII = 10 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 17.

mcqs.q: How do we write 20 in Roman numerals?
mcqs.why: 20 is two tens: 20 = 10 + 10, so 20 = X + X = XX.

mcqs.q: How do we write 7 in Roman numerals?
mcqs.why: Build 7 from 5 and ones: 7 = 5 + 1 + 1, so 7 = V + I + I = VII.

mcqs.q: A pile of dice has 1 die on the top layer, 2 in the middle and 3 at the bottom. How many dice are there, written in Roman numerals?
mcqs.why: First add the layers: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, and 6 in Roman numerals is VI.

mcqs.q: How do we write 16 in Roman numerals?
mcqs.why: Build 16 from the symbols: 16 = 10 + 5 + 1, so 16 = X + V + I = XVI.

lessons.title: Even and Odd Numbers
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A number is even if its ones digit is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. A number is odd if its ones digit is 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. Only the ones digit matters.

Worked example: Count each group and say even or odd (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: Count each group of objects in the picture.
Step 2: Look at the ones digit of each count.
Step: blocks = 3 — ones digit 3 — Odd.
Step: sharpeners = 10 — ones digit 0 — Even.
Step: bags = 4 — ones digit 4 — Even.
Step: tractors = 2 — ones digit 2 — Even.
Step: pomegranates = 5 — ones digit 5 — Odd.
Step: pizzas = 5 — ones digit 5 — Odd.
Step: peaches = 9 — ones digit 9 — Odd.
Step: pears = 8 — ones digit 8 — Even.
Answer: blocks 3 Odd; sharpeners 10 Even; bags 4 Even; tractors 2 Even; pomegranates 5 Odd; pizzas 5 Odd; peaches 9 Odd; pears 8 Even.

Worked example: Separate the even and odd numbers of the grid (Exercise 2, Q2)

Step 1: Check the ones digit of every number in the grid: 1, 8, 7, 10, 23, 14, 15, 30, 35, 42, 55, 65, 68, 72, 79, 82, 83, 91, 96, 99.
Step 2: Numbers with ones digit 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 go to the even list.
Step 3: Numbers with ones digit 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 go to the odd list.
Answer: Even: 8, 10, 14, 30, 42, 68, 72, 82, 96. Odd: 1, 7, 23, 15, 35, 55, 65, 79, 83, 91, 99.

Worked example: Write the odd numbers between (i) 4 and 16, (ii) 20 and 34 (Exercise 2, Q3)

Step 1: Odd numbers have ones digit 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.
Step 2: List them in order, without the end numbers.
Answer: (i) Between 4 and 16: 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15. (ii) Between 20 and 34: 21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 31, 33.

Worked example: Write the even numbers between (i) 1 and 10, (ii) 21 and 35 (Exercise 2, Q4)

Step 1: Even numbers have ones digit 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.
Step 2: List them in order, without the end numbers.
Answer: (i) Between 1 and 10: 2, 4, 6, 8. (ii) Between 21 and 35: 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 32, 34.

Worked example: Separate the even and odd numbers (Exercise 2, Q5)

Step 1: Check the ones digit of each number: 2, 5, 9, 18, 21, 28, 35, 56, 67, 73, 79, 80, 84, 87, 90, 93, 94, 95, 97, 99.
Answer: Even: 2, 18, 28, 56, 80, 84, 90, 94. Odd: 5, 9, 21, 35, 67, 73, 79, 87, 93, 95, 97, 99.

mcqs.q: Which of these numbers is odd?
mcqs.why: 23 has ones digit 3, which is in the odd list 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. The others end in 8, 0 and 2, so they are even.

mcqs.q: Which of these numbers is even?
mcqs.why: 96 has ones digit 6, which is in the even list 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. The others end in 7, 5 and 9, so they are odd.

mcqs.q: The number 83 is odd. Which digit tells us this?
mcqs.why: Only the ones digit matters: the ones digit of 83 is 3, and 3 is in the odd list 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.

mcqs.q: Which list shows the odd numbers between 4 and 16?
mcqs.why: Between 4 and 16 (without the end numbers), the numbers with ones digit 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 are 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15.

mcqs.q: Which list shows the even numbers between 21 and 35?
mcqs.why: Between 21 and 35, the numbers with ones digit 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 are 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 32 and 34.

mcqs.q: A picture shows 10 sharpeners. The count 10 is:
mcqs.why: The ones digit of 10 is 0, and 0 is in the even list 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, so 10 is an even number.

mcqs.q: 9 peaches are counted in the exercise. 9 is odd because its ones digit is:
mcqs.why: The ones digit of 9 is 9 itself, and 9 is in the odd list 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, so 9 is odd.

mcqs.q: The even numbers separated from the grid are 8, 10, 14, 30, 42, 68, 72, 82, 96. Which number is NOT even?
mcqs.why: 15 has ones digit 5, so it is odd and belongs to the odd list. The numbers 8, 30 and 96 all end in even digits.

mcqs.q: To decide whether a number is even or odd, we look at:
options: The first digit from the left
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes says only the ones digit matters: 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 means even, and 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 means odd.

mcqs.q: 72 is an even number because its ones digit is:
mcqs.why: The ones digit of 72 is 2, and 2 is in the even list 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, so 72 is even.

lessons.title: Numbers in Words and Numerals
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

To write a number in words, read each place from the left: ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens, ones. To write words in numerals, write the thousands part first, then the hundreds, tens and ones, keeping every place filled (use 0 for an empty place).

Worked example: Write in words: 5342, 7123, 5321, 8035, 9899, 80321 (Exercise 3, Q1)

Step 1: Read each place value from left to right.
Step 2: 5342 = Five thousand three hundred forty-two.
Step 3: 7123 = Seven thousand one hundred twenty-three.
Step 4: 5321 = Five thousand three hundred twenty-one.
Step 5: 8035 = Eight thousand thirty-five.
Step 6: 9899 = Nine thousand eight hundred ninety-nine.
Step 7: 80321 = Eighty thousand three hundred twenty-one.
Answer: 5342 = Five thousand three hundred forty-two; 7123 = Seven thousand one hundred twenty-three; 5321 = Five thousand three hundred twenty-one; 8035 = Eight thousand thirty-five; 9899 = Nine thousand eight hundred ninety-nine; 80321 = Eighty thousand three hundred twenty-one.

Worked example: Write in numerals (Exercise 3, Q2)

Step 1: Write the thousands part, then the hundreds, tens and ones.
Step 2: Five thousand eight hundred forty = 5840.
Step 3: Six thousand three hundred sixty-three = 6363.
Step 4: Thirty-two thousand three hundred eight = 32308.
Step 5: Eighty thousand five hundred eighty-seven = 80587.
Step 6: Sixty-four thousand thirty-three = 64033.
Step 7: Forty-one thousand nine hundred ninety-nine = 41999.
Answer: 5840; 6363; 32308; 80587; 64033; 41999 (in the order asked).

Worked example: Match the words with the numerals (Exercise 3, Q4)

Step 1: Convert each word form to numerals.
Step 2: Seven thousand eight hundred = 7800.
Step 3: Eighty-two thousand six hundred fifty-one = 82651.
Step 4: Fifteen thousand seven hundred sixty-three = 15763.
Step 5: Fifty-three thousand one hundred two = 53102.
Step 6: Two thousand three hundred fifty-seven = 2357.
Step 7: Five thousand three hundred twenty-six = 5326.
Step 8: Three hundred eighty-four = 384.
Answer: Seven thousand eight hundred = 7800; Eighty-two thousand six hundred fifty-one = 82651; Fifteen thousand seven hundred sixty-three = 15763; Fifty-three thousand one hundred two = 53102; Two thousand three hundred fifty-seven = 2357; Five thousand three hundred twenty-six = 5326; Three hundred eighty-four = 384.

mcqs.q: How do we write 5342 in words?
mcqs.why: Read each place from the left: 5 thousands, 3 hundreds, 4 tens and 2 ones give five thousand three hundred forty-two.

mcqs.q: How do we write 8035 in words?
mcqs.why: 8035 has 8 thousands, 0 hundreds, 3 tens and 5 ones, so it reads eight thousand thirty-five (no hundreds are spoken).

mcqs.q: Write 'Five thousand eight hundred forty' in numerals.
mcqs.why: Add the parts: 5000 + 800 + 40 = 5840, with 0 in the ones place.

mcqs.q: How do we write 80321 in words?
mcqs.why: 80321 has 80 thousands, 3 hundreds, 2 tens and 1 one, so it reads eighty thousand three hundred twenty-one.

mcqs.q: Write 'Thirty-two thousand three hundred eight' in numerals.
mcqs.why: Add the parts: 32000 + 300 + 8 = 32308. The tens place is empty, so it is filled with 0.

mcqs.q: How do we write 9899 in words?
mcqs.why: 9899 has 9 thousands, 8 hundreds, 9 tens and 9 ones, so it reads nine thousand eight hundred ninety-nine.

mcqs.q: Write 'Sixty-four thousand thirty-three' in numerals.
mcqs.why: Add the parts: 64000 + 33 = 64033. The hundreds place is empty, so it is filled with 0.

mcqs.q: Write 'Seven thousand eight hundred' in numerals.
mcqs.why: Add the parts: 7000 + 800 = 7800, with 0 in both the tens and ones places.

mcqs.q: 15763 in words is:
mcqs.why: Read the places: 15 thousands, 7 hundreds, 6 tens and 3 ones give fifteen thousand seven hundred sixty-three.

mcqs.q: How do we write 384 in words?
mcqs.why: 384 has 3 hundreds, 8 tens and 4 ones, so it reads three hundred eighty-four.

lessons.title: Expanded Form and Place Value
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

The place value of a digit = the digit x the value of its place (Ones = 1, Tens = 10, Hundreds = 100, Thousands = 1000, Ten-Thousands = 10000). The expanded form writes a number as the sum of the place values of its digits.

Worked example: Write the expanded form: 2347, 6780, 34560, 53406, 92341 (Exercise 3, Q3)

Step 1: Write each digit with its place (Ten-Th, Th, H, T, O).
Step 2: 2347 = 2 Th + 3 H + 4 T + 7 O.
Step 3: 6780 = 6 Th + 7 H + 8 T + 0 O.
Step 4: 34560 = 3 Ten-Th + 4 Th + 5 H + 6 T + 0 O.
Step 5: 53406 = 5 Ten-Th + 3 Th + 4 H + 0 T + 6 O.
Step 6: 92341 = 9 Ten-Th + 2 Th + 3 H + 4 T + 1 O.
Answer: 2347 = 2 Th + 3 H + 4 T + 7 O; 6780 = 6 Th + 7 H + 8 T + 0 O; 34560 = 3 Ten-Th + 4 Th + 5 H + 6 T + 0 O; 53406 = 5 Ten-Th + 3 Th + 4 H + 0 T + 6 O; 92341 = 9 Ten-Th + 2 Th + 3 H + 4 T + 1 O.

Worked example: In 4869, what is the value of 4 and what is the value of 6? (Exercise 3, Q5)

Step 1: In 4869, 4 is in the thousands place, so its value is 4 x 1000 = 4000.
Step 2: 6 is in the tens place, so its value is 6 x 10 = 60.
Answer: Value of 4 = 4000 (thousands); value of 6 = 60 (tens).

Worked example: Write the place value of each digit: 2357, 67815, 82301, 75389 (Exercise 3, Q6)

Step 1: Multiply each digit by its place value.
Step 2: 2357: 2000, 300, 50, 7.
Step 3: 67815: 60000, 7000, 800, 10, 5.
Step 4: 82301: 80000, 2000, 300, 0, 1.
Step 5: 75389: 70000, 5000, 300, 80, 9.
Answer: 2357: 2000, 300, 50, 7; 67815: 60000, 7000, 800, 10, 5; 82301: 80000, 2000, 300, 0, 1; 75389: 70000, 5000, 300, 80, 9.

Worked example: Write the place value of the encircled digit (Exercise 3, Q7)

Step 1: Find the place of the encircled digit and multiply the digit by that place.
Step 2: In 4567, the encircled 6 is worth 60.
Step 3: In 5327, the encircled 3 is worth 300.
Step 4: In 85761, the encircled 5 is worth 5000.
Step 5: In 70431, the encircled 1 is worth 1.
Step 6: In 67431, the encircled 6 is worth 60000.
Step 7: In 39761, the encircled 7 is worth 700.
Step 8: In 93267, the encircled 6 is worth 60.
Step 9: In 68037, the encircled 6 is worth 60000.
Step 10: In 54136, the encircled 4 is worth 4000.
Step 11: In 89791, the encircled 9 is worth 9000.
Answer: (i) 60; (ii) 300; (iii) 5000; (iv) 1; (v) 60000; (vi) 700; (vii) 60; (viii) 60000; (ix) 4000; (x) 9000.

Correction note

In (x), the encircled 9 in 89791 stands in the thousands place, so its value is 9 x 1000 = 9000. (The solved-notes page prints 900 for this part; the book page 16 shows the 9 encircled in the thousands place, so 9000 is the correct value.)

Worked example: Digit cards and train compartments (Exercise 3, Q8)

Step 1: Join the digits in order to make the number.
Step 2: Write each digit's place value.
Step 3: (i) Cards 7, 3, 8, 5, 2 make 73852; place values: 70000, 3000, 800, 50, 2.
Step 4: (ii) Compartments 4, 6, 3, 1, 9 make 46319; place values: 40000, 6000, 300, 10, 9.
Answer: (i) 73852. (ii) 46319.

Crossword activity (book pages 17–18)

Convert each clue and fill the crossword: (i) Seven thousand three hundred forty three = 7343 (already done in the book, vertical, column 3, rows 3–6). (ii) Thirty seven thousand seven hundred twenty nine = 37729 (row 3, columns 6–10). (iii) Six thousand three hundred seventy one = 6371 (column 6, rows 2–5). (iv) 4 Th + 5 H + 9 T + 8 O = 4598 (row 4, columns 8–10). (v) 7 Ten-Th + 2 Th + 2 H + 7 T + 1 O = 72271 (column 5, rows 2–6). (vi) 3 Ten-Th + 5 Th + 2 H + 7 T + 6 O = 35276 (row 4, columns 3–7). Making smaller numbers from 7152: any three different numbers made from the digits 7, 1, 5, 2 that are smaller than 7152 are correct — the book's examples are 1752, 1572 and 5127.

mcqs.q: In 4869, what is the place value of 4?
mcqs.why: In 4869 the 4 stands in the thousands place, so its value is 4 x 1000 = 4000.

mcqs.q: In 4869, what is the place value of 6?
mcqs.why: In 4869 the 6 stands in the tens place, so its value is 6 x 10 = 60.

mcqs.q: What is the expanded form of 2347?
mcqs.why: Write each digit with its own place: 2 thousands, 3 hundreds, 4 tens and 7 ones give 2 Th + 3 H + 4 T + 7 O.

mcqs.q: In 53406, what is the value of the tens digit?
mcqs.why: The tens digit of 53406 is 0, and 0 in any place has value 0 x 10 = 0.

mcqs.q: In 92341, what does the digit 9 stand for?
mcqs.why: In 92341 the 9 stands in the ten-thousands place, so its value is 9 x 10000 = 90000.

mcqs.q: In 67815, what is the place value of 8?
mcqs.why: In 67815 the 8 stands in the hundreds place, so its value is 8 x 100 = 800.

mcqs.q: Digit cards 7, 3, 8, 5, 2 are joined in order. What number do they make?
mcqs.why: Join the digits in the order given, from left to right: 7, 3, 8, 5, 2 make the number 73852.

mcqs.q: In 89791, the 9 in the thousands place has value:
mcqs.why: The 9 stands in the thousands place, so its value is 9 x 1000 = 9000, as the correction note in the lesson explains.

mcqs.q: What number is 4 Th + 5 H + 9 T + 8 O?
mcqs.why: Add the place values: 4000 + 500 + 90 + 8 = 4598.

mcqs.q: What are the place values of the digits of 75389, in order?
mcqs.why: Multiply each digit by its place: 7 x 10000 = 70000, 5 x 1000 = 5000, 3 x 100 = 300, 8 x 10 = 80 and 9 x 1 = 9.

lessons.title: Number Lines
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

On a number line, numbers increase by the same step at every mark. First find the step (subtract one mark from the next), then count forward by that step to find or place any number.

Worked example: Mark the given numbers on the number line (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: Find the step of each number line.
Step 2: Count forward by that step and mark each number.
Answer: (i) Mark 9 and 4. (ii) Mark 5, 15 and 25. (iii) Mark 6, 12, 24 and 36. (iv) Mark 4, 12, 20 and 28. (v) Mark 0, 15, 30 and 60. (vi) Mark 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15.

Worked example: Find the value of each picture on the number line (Exercise 4, Q2)

Step 1: (i) The step is 5. Count from 0: the bag stands at the 2nd mark = 2 x 5 = 10; the apple at the 4th mark = 4 x 5 = 20.
Step 2: (ii) The step is 10. Yellow box = 3 x 10 = 30; red box = 5 x 10 = 50; pink box = 7 x 10 = 70.
Step 3: (iii) The step is 2. Tractor = 3 x 2 = 6; sharpener = 5 x 2 = 10; books = 7 x 2 = 14; dice = 8 x 2 = 16.
Answer: (i) Bag = 10, apple = 20. (ii) Yellow box = 30, red box = 50, pink box = 70. (iii) Tractor = 6, sharpener = 10, books = 14, dice = 16.

Worked example: Place the number cards in the empty boxes on the number line (Exercise 4, Q3)

Step 1: (a) Line 0–24 with step 3: the marks are 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24. Put each card on its matching mark, left to right: 6, 9, 18, 21.
Step 2: (b) Line 0–800 with step 100: the marks are 0, 100, 200, ..., 800. Cards left to right: 200, 500, 700.
Answer: (a) 6, 9, 18, 21. (b) 200, 500, 700.

mcqs.q: On a number line with step 5, what number stands at the 2nd mark from 0?
mcqs.why: Multiply the mark number by the step: 2 x 5 = 10, so the bag at the 2nd mark stands for 10.

mcqs.q: On a number line with step 10, the red box stands at the 5th mark. What number is it?
mcqs.why: Multiply the mark number by the step: 5 x 10 = 50, so the red box stands for 50.

mcqs.q: On a number line with step 2, the dice stand at the 8th mark. What number is it?
mcqs.why: Multiply the mark number by the step: 8 x 2 = 16, so the dice stand for 16.

mcqs.q: A number line goes from 0 to 24 with step 3. Which number is NOT one of its marks?
mcqs.why: The marks are the multiples of 3: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24. The number 10 is not a multiple of 3, so it is not a mark.

mcqs.q: On a 0 to 800 number line with step 100, what number stands at the 5th mark?
mcqs.why: Multiply the mark number by the step: 5 x 100 = 500, so the 5th mark is 500.

mcqs.q: How do we find the step of a number line?
options: Subtract one mark from the next mark
Count how many marks there are
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: the step is the gap between two marks next to each other, found by subtracting one mark from the next.

mcqs.q: On a number line with step 5, the apple stands at the 4th mark. What number is it?
mcqs.why: Multiply the mark number by the step: 4 x 5 = 20, so the apple stands for 20.

mcqs.q: On a number line with step 3, at which mark does 18 stand?
mcqs.why: Divide the number by the step to find its mark: 6 x 3 = 18, so 18 stands at the 6th mark.

mcqs.q: On a number line with step 2, the sharpener stands at the 5th mark. What number is it?
mcqs.why: Multiply the mark number by the step: 5 x 2 = 10, so the sharpener stands for 10.

mcqs.q: On a number line with step 10, the pink box stands at the 7th mark. What number is it?
mcqs.why: Multiply the mark number by the step: 7 x 10 = 70, so the pink box stands for 70.

lessons.title: Comparing and Ordering Numbers
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

To compare two numbers, compare the hundreds digits first, then the tens, then the ones. The bigger digit at the first place where they differ makes that number greater. Ascending order means smallest to greatest; descending order means greatest to smallest.

Worked example: Put the correct symbol (>, < or =) (Exercise 5, Q1)

Step 1: Compare the hundreds digits first, then tens, then ones.
Step 2: 873 > 426.
Step 3: 694 < 706.
Step 4: 857 = 857.
Step 5: 978 > 824.
Step 6: 574 = 574.
Step 7: 819 > 817.
Answer: 873 > 426; 694 < 706; 857 = 857; 978 > 824; 574 = 574; 819 > 817.

Greater number in each pair (Exercise 5, Q2)

Compare hundreds, then tens, then ones in each pair as printed in the book. The greater numbers are: 671; 249; 374; 738; 937; 877.

Worked example: Write in ascending and descending order (Exercise 5, Q3)

Step 1: Ascending means smallest to greatest. Step 2: Descending means greatest to smallest.
Step: (i) Ascending: 51, 61, 71, 91. Descending: 91, 71, 61, 51.
Step: (ii) Ascending: 41, 52, 67, 73, 85. Descending: 85, 73, 67, 52, 41.
Step: (iii) Ascending: 321, 346, 451, 536. Descending: 536, 451, 346, 321.
Step: (iv) Ascending: 231, 278, 543, 698, 731. Descending: 731, 698, 543, 278, 231.
Step: (v) Ascending: 335, 345, 471, 472, 476. Descending: 476, 472, 471, 345, 335.
Answer: (i) Asc: 51, 61, 71, 91. Desc: 91, 71, 61, 51. (ii) Asc: 41, 52, 67, 73, 85. Desc: 85, 73, 67, 52, 41. (iii) Asc: 321, 346, 451, 536. Desc: 536, 451, 346, 321. (iv) Asc: 231, 278, 543, 698, 731. Desc: 731, 698, 543, 278, 231. (v) Asc: 335, 345, 471, 472, 476. Desc: 476, 472, 471, 345, 335.

Worked example: Write five numbers less than 321, in ascending and descending order (Exercise 5, Q4)

Step 1: Any five numbers below 321 are correct; the book's example uses 301, 305, 310, 315, 320.
Step 2: Ascending: 301, 305, 310, 315, 320.
Step 3: Descending: 320, 315, 310, 305, 301.
Answer: Ascending: 301, 305, 310, 315, 320. Descending: 320, 315, 310, 305, 301.

mcqs.q: Put the correct symbol: 873 ___ 426
mcqs.why: Compare the hundreds digits first: 8 is greater than 4, so 873 > 426 without looking at the other digits.

mcqs.q: Put the correct symbol: 694 ___ 706
mcqs.why: Compare the hundreds digits first: 6 is smaller than 7, so 694 < 706.

mcqs.q: Put the correct symbol: 819 ___ 817
mcqs.why: The hundreds and tens digits are equal, so compare the ones: 9 is greater than 7, so 819 > 817.

mcqs.q: Write 51, 91, 61, 71 in ascending order.
mcqs.why: Ascending order means smallest to greatest: 51 is smallest, then 61, then 71, and 91 is greatest.

mcqs.q: Write 41, 52, 67, 73, 85 in descending order.
mcqs.why: Descending order means greatest to smallest: 85 is greatest, then 73, 67, 52, and 41 is smallest.

mcqs.q: Write 321, 536, 346, 451 in ascending order.
mcqs.why: Compare hundreds first: 321 and 346 start with 3, and 321 < 346 by tens; then 451, then 536. So the order is 321, 346, 451, 536.

mcqs.q: Which is the smallest number: 335, 345, 471, 472, 476?
mcqs.why: 335 and 345 have hundreds digit 3, smaller than 4. Between them the tens digits decide: 3 is smaller than 4, so 335 is the smallest.

mcqs.q: The book's example uses five numbers less than 321. In ascending order they are:
mcqs.why: All five numbers 301, 305, 310, 315, 320 are less than 321, and ascending order lists them smallest to greatest.

mcqs.q: To compare two numbers, which digits do we compare first?
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: compare the hundreds digits first, then the tens, then the ones; the first place where they differ decides.

mcqs.q: Put the correct symbol: 978 ___ 824
mcqs.why: Compare the hundreds digits first: 9 is greater than 8, so 978 > 824.

lessons.title: Rounding Numbers
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

To round to the nearest 10, look at the ones digit: 5 or more rounds up to the next ten; less than 5 rounds down. To round to the nearest 100, look at the tens digit the same way. The book's own rule (book page 30): a small number such as 37 is nearer to 0 than to 100, so it rounds to 0 to the nearest 100.

Worked example: Round to the nearest 10 and to the nearest 100: 26, 52, 327, 385, 750 (Exercise 6, Q1)

Step 1: For the nearest 10, look at the ones digit: 5 or more rounds up.
Step 2: For the nearest 100, look at the tens digit: 5 or more rounds up.
Step: 26 — ones digit 6 gives nearest 10 = 30; tens digit 2 gives nearest 100 = 0.
Step: 52 — ones digit 2 gives nearest 10 = 50; tens digit 5 gives nearest 100 = 100.
Step: 327 — ones digit 7 gives nearest 10 = 330; tens digit 2 gives nearest 100 = 300.
Step: 385 — ones digit 5 gives nearest 10 = 390; tens digit 8 gives nearest 100 = 400.
Step: 750 — ones digit 0 gives nearest 10 = 750; tens digit 5 gives nearest 100 = 800.
Answer: 26 to 30, 0; 52 to 50, 100; 327 to 330, 300; 385 to 390, 400; 750 to 750, 800.

Worked example: Match each number with its nearest 10 and nearest 100 (Exercise 6, Q2)

Step 1: Round each number to the nearest 10 by its ones digit.
Step 2: Round each number to the nearest 100 by its tens digit.
Answer: Nearest 10: 19 to 20, 32 to 30, 41 to 40, 52 to 50, 61 to 60, 76 to 80, 95 to 100. Nearest 100: 101 to 100, 256 to 300, 384 to 400, 517 to 500, 649 to 600, 739 to 700, 850 to 900.

Worked example: On the number line, 26 rounds to which nearest 10? (Exercise 6, Q3)

Step 1: On the number line, 26 lies between 20 and 30.
Step 2: 26 is nearer to 30 than to 20.
Answer: 30.

Worked example: On the number line, 735 rounds to which nearest 100? (Exercise 6, Q4)

Step 1: On the number line, 735 lies between 700 and 800.
Step 2: 735 is nearer to 700 than to 800.
Answer: 700.

lessons.title: Adding 4-Digit Numbers Without Carrying
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Add column by column from the right: ones, then tens, then hundreds, then thousands. If a column adds to 10 or more, write the ones digit of that sum and carry 1 to the next column.

Worked example: 6643 + 3215 (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 3 + 5 = 8.
Step 2: tens: 4 + 1 = 5.
Step 3: hundreds: 6 + 2 = 8.
Step 4: thousands: 6 + 3 = 9.
Answer: 6643 + 3215 = 9858.

Worked example: 5137 + 3542 (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 7 + 2 = 9.
Step 2: tens: 3 + 4 = 7.
Step 3: hundreds: 1 + 5 = 6.
Step 4: thousands: 5 + 3 = 8.
Answer: 5137 + 3542 = 8679.

Worked example: 7256 + 1423 (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 6 + 3 = 9.
Step 2: tens: 5 + 2 = 7.
Step 3: hundreds: 2 + 4 = 6.
Step 4: thousands: 7 + 1 = 8.
Answer: 7256 + 1423 = 8679.

Worked example: 6795 + 2104 (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 5 + 4 = 9.
Step 2: tens: 9 + 0 = 9.
Step 3: hundreds: 7 + 1 = 8.
Step 4: thousands: 6 + 2 = 8.
Answer: 6795 + 2104 = 8899.

Worked example: 7000 + 2137 (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 0 + 7 = 7.
Step 2: tens: 0 + 3 = 3.
Step 3: hundreds: 0 + 1 = 1.
Step 4: thousands: 7 + 2 = 9.
Answer: 7000 + 2137 = 9137.

Worked example: 4000 + 3154 (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 0 + 4 = 4.
Step 2: tens: 0 + 5 = 5.
Step 3: hundreds: 0 + 1 = 1.
Step 4: thousands: 4 + 3 = 7.
Answer: 4000 + 3154 = 7154.

mcqs.why: Add column by column: ones 3 + 5 = 8, tens 4 + 1 = 5, hundreds 6 + 2 = 8, thousands 6 + 3 = 9, giving 9858.
Add column by column: ones 7 + 2 = 9, tens 3 + 4 = 7, hundreds 1 + 5 = 6, thousands 5 + 3 = 8, giving 8679.
Add column by column: ones 6 + 3 = 9, tens 5 + 2 = 7, hundreds 2 + 4 = 6, thousands 7 + 1 = 8, giving 8679.
Add column by column: ones 5 + 4 = 9, tens 9 + 0 = 9, hundreds 7 + 1 = 8, thousands 6 + 2 = 8, giving 8899.
Add column by column: ones 0 + 7 = 7, tens 0 + 3 = 3, hundreds 0 + 1 = 1, thousands 7 + 2 = 9, giving 9137.
Add column by column: ones 0 + 4 = 4, tens 0 + 5 = 5, hundreds 0 + 1 = 1, thousands 4 + 3 = 7, giving 7154.

mcqs.q: When we add numbers in columns, we start from:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: always add column by column from the right, starting with the ones, then tens, hundreds and thousands.

mcqs.q: In 6643 + 3215, what is the ones column sum?
mcqs.why: The ones digits are 3 and 5, and 3 + 5 = 8, so the ones column sum is 8.

mcqs.q: In 6795 + 2104, what is the hundreds column sum?
mcqs.why: The hundreds digits are 7 and 1, and 7 + 1 = 8, so the hundreds column sum is 8.

mcqs.q: What is 5137 + 3542? (Check: this sum is the same as 7256 + 1423.)
mcqs.why: Work it out: ones 7 + 2 = 9, tens 3 + 4 = 7, hundreds 1 + 5 = 6, thousands 5 + 3 = 8, giving 8679.

lessons.title: Adding 4-Digit Numbers With Carrying
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

With carrying, a column sum of 10 or more gives a carried 1 that is added into the next column. Always add the carried 1 before writing that column's digit.

Worked example: 5794 + 3825 (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: ones: 4 + 5 = 9.
Step 2: tens: 9 + 2 = 11 — write 1, carry 1.
Step 3: hundreds: 7 + 8 + 1 (carried) = 16 — write 6, carry 1.
Step 4: thousands: 5 + 3 + 1 (carried) = 9.
Answer: 5794 + 3825 = 9619.

Worked example: 4752 + 3596 (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: ones: 2 + 6 = 8.
Step 2: tens: 5 + 9 = 14 — write 4, carry 1.
Step 3: hundreds: 7 + 5 + 1 (carried) = 13 — write 3, carry 1.
Step 4: thousands: 4 + 3 + 1 (carried) = 8.
Answer: 4752 + 3596 = 8348.

Worked example: 5496 + 2179 (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: ones: 6 + 9 = 15 — write 5, carry 1.
Step 2: tens: 9 + 7 + 1 (carried) = 17 — write 7, carry 1.
Step 3: hundreds: 4 + 1 + 1 (carried) = 6.
Step 4: thousands: 5 + 2 = 7.
Answer: 5496 + 2179 = 7675.

Worked example: 6243 + 5727 (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: ones: 3 + 7 = 10 — write 0, carry 1.
Step 2: tens: 4 + 2 + 1 (carried) = 7.
Step 3: hundreds: 2 + 7 = 9.
Step 4: thousands: 6 + 5 = 11 — write 1, carry 1.
Step 5: ten-thousands: 0 + 0 + 1 (carried) = 1.
Answer: 6243 + 5727 = 11970.

Worked example: 6495 + 2156 (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: ones: 5 + 6 = 11 — write 1, carry 1.
Step 2: tens: 9 + 5 + 1 (carried) = 15 — write 5, carry 1.
Step 3: hundreds: 4 + 1 + 1 (carried) = 6.
Step 4: thousands: 6 + 2 = 8.
Answer: 6495 + 2156 = 8651.

Worked example: 5676 + 3864 (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: ones: 6 + 4 = 10 — write 0, carry 1.
Step 2: tens: 7 + 6 + 1 (carried) = 14 — write 4, carry 1.
Step 3: hundreds: 6 + 8 + 1 (carried) = 15 — write 5, carry 1.
Step 4: thousands: 5 + 3 + 1 (carried) = 9.
Answer: 5676 + 3864 = 9540.

mcqs.why: Ones 4 + 5 = 9; tens 9 + 2 = 11, write 1 carry 1; hundreds 7 + 8 + 1 = 16, write 6 carry 1; thousands 5 + 3 + 1 = 9, giving 9619.
Ones 2 + 6 = 8; tens 5 + 9 = 14, write 4 carry 1; hundreds 7 + 5 + 1 = 13, write 3 carry 1; thousands 4 + 3 + 1 = 8, giving 8348.
Ones 6 + 9 = 15, write 5 carry 1; tens 9 + 7 + 1 = 17, write 7 carry 1; hundreds 4 + 1 + 1 = 6; thousands 5 + 2 = 7, giving 7675.
Ones 3 + 7 = 10, write 0 carry 1; tens 4 + 2 + 1 = 7; hundreds 2 + 7 = 9; thousands 6 + 5 = 11, write 1 and carry 1 to make a new ten-thousands digit, giving 11970.
Ones 5 + 6 = 11, write 1 carry 1; tens 9 + 5 + 1 = 15, write 5 carry 1; hundreds 4 + 1 + 1 = 6; thousands 6 + 2 = 8, giving 8651.
Ones 6 + 4 = 10, write 0 carry 1; tens 7 + 6 + 1 = 14, write 4 carry 1; hundreds 6 + 8 + 1 = 15, write 5 carry 1; thousands 5 + 3 + 1 = 9, giving 9540.

mcqs.q: In 5496 + 2179, the ones column adds to 6 + 9 = 15. What do we do?
mcqs.why: A column sum of 15 has ones digit 5 and tens digit 1: we write the 5 in the ones column and carry the 1 to the tens column.

mcqs.q: Why does 6243 + 5727 have a 5-digit answer?
options: The thousands column adds to 11 and makes a new ten-thousands digit
mcqs.why: In the thousands column, 6 + 5 = 11: we write 1 and carry 1, and that carried 1 becomes a new ten-thousands digit, so the answer 11970 has 5 digits.

mcqs.q: In 5676 + 3864, what is the tens column total, including the carried 1?
mcqs.why: The tens digits are 7 and 6, plus the 1 carried from the ones column: 7 + 6 + 1 = 14, so we write 4 and carry 1.

mcqs.q: A column adds to 10 or more. What must we do?
options: Write the whole sum in that column
Write the ones digit of the sum and carry 1 to the next column
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: when a column adds to 10 or more, write the ones digit of that sum and carry 1 into the next column, adding it there first.

lessons.title: Addition Word Problems and Mental Addition
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

In a word problem, look for the joining words — in all, together, total — then add the two numbers column by column. For mental addition of 2-digit numbers, add the tens first, then the ones.

Worked example: Trees in two parks: 3454 trees and 2345 trees (Exercise 1, Q3)

Step 1: ones: 4 + 5 = 9.
Step 2: tens: 5 + 4 = 9.
Step 3: hundreds: 4 + 3 = 7.
Step 4: thousands: 3 + 2 = 5.
Answer: 5799 trees in all.

Worked example: Add Rs 6758 + Rs 3441 (Exercise 1, Q4)

Step 1: ones: 8 + 1 = 9.
Step 2: tens: 5 + 4 = 9.
Step 3: hundreds: 7 + 4 = 11 — write 1, carry 1.
Step 4: thousands: 6 + 3 + 1 (carried) = 10 — write 0, carry 1.
Step 5: ten-thousands: 0 + 0 + 1 (carried) = 1.
Answer: Rs 10199.

Step 1: ones: 6 + 3 = 9.
Step 2: tens: 3 + 5 = 8.
Step 3: hundreds: 5 + 2 = 7.
Step 4: thousands: 4 + 3 = 7.
Answer: 7789 people visit in all.

Step 1: ones: 0 + 0 = 0.
Step 2: tens: 4 + 2 = 6.
Step 3: hundreds: 5 + 1 = 6.
Step 4: thousands: 6 + 2 = 8.

Step 2: tens: 5 + 3 = 8.

lessons.title: Subtracting 4-Digit Numbers
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Subtract column by column from the right: ones, then tens, then hundreds, then thousands. If the top digit of a column is smaller than the bottom digit, borrow 1 from the next column (the borrowed 1 is worth 10 in this column).

Worked example: 3546 − 2324 (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 6 − 4 = 2.
Step 2: tens: 4 − 2 = 2.
Step 3: hundreds: 5 − 3 = 2.
Step 4: thousands: 3 − 2 = 1.
Answer: 3546 − 2324 = 1222.

Worked example: 5796 − 3453 (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 6 − 3 = 3.
Step 2: tens: 9 − 5 = 4.
Step 3: hundreds: 7 − 4 = 3.
Step 4: thousands: 5 − 3 = 2.
Answer: 5796 − 3453 = 2343.

Worked example: 6354 − 4041 (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 2: tens: 5 − 4 = 1.
Step 3: hundreds: 3 − 0 = 3.
Step 4: thousands: 6 − 4 = 2.
Answer: 6354 − 4041 = 2313.

Worked example: 8764 − 3653 (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 2: tens: 6 − 5 = 1.
Step 3: hundreds: 7 − 6 = 1.
Step 4: thousands: 8 − 3 = 5.
Answer: 8764 − 3653 = 5111.

Worked example: 4754 − 3532 (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 4 − 2 = 2.
Step 2: tens: 5 − 3 = 2.
Step 3: hundreds: 7 − 5 = 2.
Step 4: thousands: 4 − 3 = 1.
Answer: 4754 − 3532 = 1222.

Worked example: 9876 − 6754 (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 2: tens: 6 is smaller than 7, so borrow 1 from the next column: 16 − 7 = 9.
Step 3: hundreds: 6 is smaller than 9, so borrow 1 from the next column: 16 − 9 = 7.

lessons.title: Subtraction Word Problems
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Words such as left, remaining, how many more tell us to subtract. Subtract the smaller number from the bigger number, column by column, borrowing when needed.

Worked example: A book has 1535 pages; 424 pages have been read (Exercise 2, Q3)

Step 1: ones: 5 − 4 = 1.
Step 2: tens: 3 − 2 = 1.
Step 3: hundreds: 5 − 4 = 1.
Step 4: thousands: 1 − 0 = 1.
Answer: 1111 pages left to read.

Worked example: Subtract Rs 6456 − Rs 4340 (Exercise 2, Q4)

Step 1: ones: 6 − 0 = 6.
Step 2: tens: 5 − 4 = 1.
Step 3: hundreds: 4 − 3 = 1.
Step 4: thousands: 6 − 4 = 2.
Answer: Rs 2116.

Worked example: A town has 6753 people; 3985 are women (Exercise 2, Q5)

Step 1: ones: 3 is smaller than 5, so borrow 1 from the next column: 13 − 5 = 8.
Step 2: tens: 4 is smaller than 8, so borrow 1 from the next column: 14 − 8 = 6.
Step 3: hundreds: 6 is smaller than 9, so borrow 1 from the next column: 16 − 9 = 7.
Step 4: thousands: 5 − 3 = 2.
Answer: 2768 men.

Worked example: A farmer has 7516 goats and sells 5728 (Exercise 2, Q6)

Step 1: ones: 6 is smaller than 8, so borrow 1 from the next column: 16 − 8 = 8.
Step 2: tens: 0 is smaller than 2, so borrow 1 from the next column: 10 − 2 = 8.
Step 3: hundreds: 4 is smaller than 7, so borrow 1 from the next column: 14 − 7 = 7.
Step 4: thousands: 6 − 5 = 1.
Answer: 1788 goats left.

mcqs.q: A book has 1535 pages. 424 pages have been read. How many pages are left to read?
mcqs.why: The word 'left' tells us to subtract: ones 5 - 4 = 1, tens 3 - 2 = 1, hundreds 5 - 4 = 1, thousands 1 - 0 = 1, giving 1111 pages left.

mcqs.q: Subtract Rs 6456 - Rs 4340.
mcqs.why: Subtract column by column: ones 6 - 0 = 6, tens 5 - 4 = 1, hundreds 4 - 3 = 1, thousands 6 - 4 = 2, giving Rs 2116.

mcqs.q: A town has 6753 people, and 3985 of them are women. How many are men?
mcqs.why: Subtract the women from the total, borrowing each time: ones 13 - 5 = 8, tens 14 - 8 = 6, hundreds 16 - 9 = 7, thousands 5 - 3 = 2, giving 2768 men.

mcqs.q: A farmer has 7516 goats and sells 5728 of them. How many goats are left?
mcqs.why: Subtract, borrowing each time: ones 16 - 8 = 8, tens 10 - 2 = 8, hundreds 14 - 7 = 7, thousands 6 - 5 = 1, giving 1788 goats left.

mcqs.q: Which words in a word problem tell us to subtract?
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: words such as 'left', 'remaining' and 'how many more' tell us the problem is a subtraction.

mcqs.q: In 6753 - 3985, the ones column is 3 - 5. After borrowing, it becomes:
mcqs.why: 3 is smaller than 5, so we borrow 1 from the tens column; the borrowed 1 is worth 10 here, giving 13 - 5 = 8.

mcqs.q: In 7516 - 5728, after borrowing, the hundreds column becomes 14 - 7. What is the result?
mcqs.why: The hundreds digit 5 lent 1 to the tens column, leaving 4, which is smaller than 7, so it borrows 1 itself: 14 - 7 = 7.

mcqs.q: When we subtract, we take the smaller number away from:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: subtract the smaller number from the bigger number, column by column, borrowing when needed.

mcqs.q: A book has 1535 pages and 424 are read. To find the pages left, we use:
mcqs.why: Pages left means taking the read pages away from the whole book, and the word 'left' is a subtraction word in the notes.

mcqs.q: A town has 6753 people and 3985 are women. Which sum finds the number of men?
mcqs.why: The men are what remains after the women are taken away from the total, so the sum is 6753 - 3985, which gives 2768 men.

lessons.title: Multiplication Tables of 6, 7, 8 and 9
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A multiplication table is made by repeated addition: 6 x 4 means 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24. Learn the tables of 6, 7, 8 and 9 up to 10.

The tables of 6, 7, 8 and 9 (Exercise 3, Q1)

lessons.title: Multiplying a 2-Digit Number by a 1-Digit Number
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

To multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number: multiply the ones digit first, carry the ten if the product is 10 or more, then multiply the tens digit and add the carry. Two key facts: any number x 0 = 0, and any number x 1 = the number itself.

Worked example: 24 x 3 (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 4 x 3 = 12 — write 2, carry 1.
Step 2: tens: 2 x 3 + 1 (carried) = 7.
Answer: 24 x 3 = 72.

Worked example: 35 x 4 (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 5 x 4 = 20 — write 0, carry 2.
Step 2: tens: 3 x 4 + 2 (carried) = 14 — write 4, carry 1.
Answer: 35 x 4 = 140.

Worked example: 32 x 5 (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 2 x 5 = 10 — write 0, carry 1.
Step 2: tens: 3 x 5 + 1 (carried) = 16 — write 6, carry 1.
Answer: 32 x 5 = 160.

Worked example: 38 x 6 (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 8 x 6 = 48 — write 8, carry 4.
Step 2: tens: 3 x 6 + 4 (carried) = 22 — write 2, carry 2.
Answer: 38 x 6 = 228.

Worked example: 45 x 7 (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 5 x 7 = 35 — write 5, carry 3.
Step 2: tens: 4 x 7 + 3 (carried) = 31 — write 1, carry 3.
Answer: 45 x 7 = 315.

Worked example: 48 x 8 (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 8 x 8 = 64 — write 4, carry 6.
Step 2: tens: 4 x 8 + 6 (carried) = 38 — write 8, carry 3.
Answer: 48 x 8 = 384.

Worked example: 54 x 9 (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 4 x 9 = 36 — write 6, carry 3.
Step 2: tens: 5 x 9 + 3 (carried) = 48 — write 8, carry 4.
Answer: 54 x 9 = 486.

Worked example: 56 x 7 (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 6 x 7 = 42 — write 2, carry 4.
Step 2: tens: 5 x 7 + 4 (carried) = 39 — write 9, carry 3.
Answer: 56 x 7 = 392.

Worked example: 62 x 6 (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: ones: 2 x 6 = 12 — write 2, carry 1.
Step 2: tens: 6 x 6 + 1 (carried) = 37 — write 7, carry 3.
Answer: 62 x 6 = 372.

Worked example: Multiply using the tables (Exercise 4, Q2)

Step 1: Recall the table facts.
Step: 7 x 6 = 42.
Step: 5 x 6 = 30.
Step: 4 x 7 = 28.
Step: 9 x 7 = 63.
Step: 4 x 9 = 36.
Step: 8 x 7 = 56.
Answer: 7 x 6 = 42; 5 x 6 = 30; 4 x 7 = 28; 9 x 7 = 63; 4 x 9 = 36; 8 x 7 = 56.

Multiplying by 0 and by 1 (Exercise 4, Q3)

5 x 0 = 0. 35 x 0 = 0. 45 x 0 = 0. 48 x 1 = 48. 1 x 57 = 57. 31 x 1 = 31.

Worked example: Multiply mentally (Exercise 4, Q4)

Step 1: Use the tables in your head.
Step: 4 x 9 = 36.
Step: 5 x 4 = 20.
Step: 6 x 3 = 18.
Step: 6 x 5 = 30.
Step: 8 x 4 = 32.
Step: 7 x 5 = 35.
Answer: 4 x 9 = 36; 5 x 4 = 20; 6 x 3 = 18; 6 x 5 = 30; 8 x 4 = 32; 7 x 5 = 35.

Worked example: Multiply Rs 24 x 4 (Exercise 4, Q5)

Step 1: ones: 4 x 4 = 16 — write 6, carry 1.
Step 2: tens: 2 x 4 + 1 (carried) = 9.
Answer: Rs 96.

Worked example: There are 52 weeks in a year. How many weeks in 7 years? (Exercise 4, Q6)

Step 1: ones: 2 x 7 = 14 — write 4, carry 1.
Step 2: tens: 5 x 7 + 1 (carried) = 36 — write 6, carry 3.
Answer: 364 weeks.

Worked example: 28 trees in one row. How many trees in 5 rows? (Exercise 4, Q7)

Step 1: ones: 8 x 5 = 40 — write 0, carry 4.
Step 2: tens: 2 x 5 + 4 (carried) = 14 — write 4, carry 1.
Answer: 140 trees.

Worked example: A car travels 62 km in 1 litre. How far in 4 litres? (Exercise 4, Q8)

Step 1: ones: 2 x 4 = 8.
Step 2: tens: 6 x 4 = 24 — write 4, carry 2.
Answer: 248 km.

lessons.title: Division Using Multiplication Tables
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Division is sharing equally — and it is the reverse of multiplication. To divide, ask: which table fact gives this number? Example: 42 ÷ 6 — 6 x 7 = 42, so 42 ÷ 6 = 7.

Worked example: Divide (Exercise 5)

Step 1: Use the multiplication tables in reverse.
Step: 20 ÷ 4: 4 x 5 = 20, so 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
Step: 25 ÷ 5: 5 x 5 = 25, so 25 ÷ 5 = 5.
Step: 42 ÷ 6: 6 x 7 = 42, so 42 ÷ 6 = 7.
Step: 49 ÷ 7: 7 x 7 = 49, so 49 ÷ 7 = 7.
Step: 72 ÷ 8: 8 x 9 = 72, so 72 ÷ 8 = 9.
Step: 81 ÷ 9: 9 x 9 = 81, so 81 ÷ 9 = 9.
Step: 48 ÷ 4: 4 x 12 = 48, so 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
Step: 72 ÷ 6: 6 x 12 = 72, so 72 ÷ 6 = 12.
Step: 84 ÷ 7: 7 x 12 = 84, so 84 ÷ 7 = 12.
Step: 51 ÷ 3: 3 x 17 = 51, so 51 ÷ 3 = 17.
Step: 96 ÷ 8: 8 x 12 = 96, so 96 ÷ 8 = 12.
Step: 99 ÷ 9: 9 x 11 = 99, so 99 ÷ 9 = 11.
Step: 4 ÷ 2: 2 x 2 = 4, so 4 ÷ 2 = 2.
Step: 8 ÷ 4: 4 x 2 = 8, so 8 ÷ 4 = 2.
Step: 9 ÷ 3: 3 x 3 = 9, so 9 ÷ 3 = 3.
Answer: 20 ÷ 4 = 5; 25 ÷ 5 = 5; 42 ÷ 6 = 7; 49 ÷ 7 = 7; 72 ÷ 8 = 9; 81 ÷ 9 = 9; 48 ÷ 4 = 12; 72 ÷ 6 = 12; 84 ÷ 7 = 12; 51 ÷ 3 = 17; 96 ÷ 8 = 12; 99 ÷ 9 = 11; 4 ÷ 2 = 2; 8 ÷ 4 = 2; 9 ÷ 3 = 3.

Worked example: 96 students stand in 6 equal rows (Exercise 5)

Step 1: Divide: 96 ÷ 6.
Step 2: 6 x 16 = 96, so 96 ÷ 6 = 16.
Answer: 16 students in each row.

Worked example: A man covers 56 km in 4 days, the same distance each day (Exercise 5)

Step 1: Divide: 56 ÷ 4.
Step 2: 4 x 14 = 56, so 56 ÷ 4 = 14.
Answer: 14 km per day.

Worked example: 70 pencils are packed equally in 5 packets (Exercise 5)

Step 1: Divide: 70 ÷ 5.
Step 2: 5 x 14 = 70, so 70 ÷ 5 = 14.
Answer: 14 pencils in each packet.

Worked example: 91 rupees buy 7 notebooks of equal price (Exercise 5)

Step 1: Divide: 91 ÷ 7.
Step 2: 7 x 13 = 91, so 91 ÷ 7 = 13.
Answer: Rs 13 per notebook.

Worked example: 48 pencils are shared equally among 8 children (Exercise 5)

Step 1: Divide: 48 ÷ 8.
Step 2: 8 x 6 = 48, so 48 ÷ 8 = 6.
Answer: 6 pencils for each child.

lessons.title: Fractions — Numerator and Denominator
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A fraction is a part of a whole divided into equal parts. The number on top is the numerator — it tells how many parts are taken. The number below the line is the denominator — it tells into how many equal parts the whole is divided.

Worked example: Write the numerator and denominator of each fraction (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: The top number is the numerator; the bottom number is the denominator.
Step: 2/7 — numerator 2, denominator 7.
Step: 3/7 — numerator 3, denominator 7.
Step: 5/8 — numerator 5, denominator 8.
Step: 2/5 — numerator 2, denominator 5.
Step: 10/13 — numerator 10, denominator 13.
Step: 9/10 — numerator 9, denominator 10.
Step: 1/8 — numerator 1, denominator 8.
Step: 2/3 — numerator 2, denominator 3.
Step: 4/7 — numerator 4, denominator 7.
Step: 3/4 — numerator 3, denominator 4.
Answer: 2/7 (numerator 2, denominator 7); 3/7 (numerator 3, denominator 7); 5/8 (numerator 5, denominator 8); 2/5 (numerator 2, denominator 5); 10/13 (numerator 10, denominator 13); 9/10 (numerator 9, denominator 10); 1/8 (numerator 1, denominator 8); 2/3 (numerator 2, denominator 3); 4/7 (numerator 4, denominator 7); 3/4 (numerator 3, denominator 4).

Worked example: Write the fraction of the coloured part (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: Count all the equal parts of the figure — that is the denominator.
Step 2: Count the coloured parts — that is the numerator.
Step 3: First circle: 1/4 (given in the book). Second circle: 3/8. Third circle: 1/3.
Step 4: First grid: 5/16. Second grid: 4/16.
Step 5: Square of 8 triangles: 5 green triangles out of 8 = 5/8.
Answer: Circles: 1/4, 3/8, 1/3. Grids: 5/16, 4/16. Triangles: 5/8.

Worked example: Colour the given fraction of each figure: 2/3, 3/4, 3/8, 3/6 (Exercise 1, Q3)

Step 1: Divide the figure into the denominator's number of equal parts.
Step 2: Colour the numerator's number of parts.
Answer: Colour 2 of 3 parts for 2/3; 3 of 4 triangles for 3/4; 3 of 8 sectors for 3/8; 3 of 6 parts for 3/6.

Worked example: Write the fraction shown by each figure (Exercise 1, Q4)

Step 1: Count the total parts and the shaded parts of each figure.
Answer: (i) 4/11 (given in the book); (ii) 3/11; (iii) 4/9; (iv) 5/7.

Worked example: Match each figure with its fraction (Exercise 1, Q5)

Step 1: Count the shaded parts and the total parts of each figure, then match.
Answer: (i) 2/3; (ii) 1/4; (iii) 2/5; (iv) 3/8; (v) 2/8; (vi) 3/4.

lessons.title: Proper and Improper Fractions
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A proper fraction has its numerator smaller than its denominator (3/4). An improper fraction has its numerator greater than or equal to its denominator (4/3, 7/7).

Worked example: Tell whether each fraction is proper or improper (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: If the numerator is smaller than the denominator, the fraction is proper.
Step 2: If the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator, it is improper (the book's Key Fact).
Step: (i) 3/4: numerator 3 < denominator 4 — proper.
Step: (ii) 4/5: numerator 4 < denominator 5 — proper.
Step: (iii) 4/3: numerator 4 ≥ denominator 3 — improper.
Step: (iv) 4/9: numerator 4 < denominator 9 — proper.
Step: (v) 7/5: numerator 7 ≥ denominator 5 — improper.
Step: (vi) 9/5: numerator 9 ≥ denominator 5 — improper.
Step: (vii) 8/9: numerator 8 < denominator 9 — proper.
Step: (viii) 3/7: numerator 3 < denominator 7 — proper.
Step: (ix) 7/7: numerator 7 ≥ denominator 7 — improper.
Answer: 3/4 proper; 4/5 proper; 4/3 improper; 4/9 proper; 7/5 improper; 9/5 improper; 8/9 proper; 3/7 proper; 7/7 improper.

Worked example: Separate into proper and improper fractions (Exercise 2, Q2)

Step 1: Compare the numerator and denominator of each fraction.
Answer: Proper: 4/5, 7/12, 7/19, 8/15, 7/9. Improper: 13/6, 14/5, 9/4, 8/5, 7/4.

lessons.title: Equivalent Fractions
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Equivalent fractions name the same part of a whole. To make an equivalent fraction, multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number. You may also divide both by the same number: 3/6 ÷ 3 = 1/2.

Worked example: Match each fraction with its equivalent fraction (Exercise 3, Q1)

Step 1: Multiply the numerator and denominator by the same number and match.
Step: 3/5 = 6/10.
Step: 5/9 = 10/18.
Step: 4/7 = 8/14.
Step: 3/6 = 1/2.
Step: 3/8 = 9/24.
Step: 5/7 = 15/21.
Answer: 3/5 = 6/10; 5/9 = 10/18; 4/7 = 8/14; 3/6 = 1/2; 3/8 = 9/24; 5/7 = 15/21.

Worked example: Write three equivalent fractions for each (Exercise 3, Q2)

Step 1: Multiply the numerator and denominator by 2, then by 3, then by 4.
Step: 5/6 x2, x3, x4 gives 10/12, 15/18, 20/24.
Step: 2/3 x2, x3, x4 gives 4/6, 6/9, 8/12.
Step: 1/4 x2, x3, x4 gives 2/8, 3/12, 4/16.
Step: 5/8 x2, x3, x4 gives 10/16, 15/24, 20/32.
Step: 3/5 x2, x3, x4 gives 6/10, 9/15, 12/20.
Step: 2/5 x2, x3, x4 gives 4/10, 6/15, 8/20.
Answer: (i) 5/6: 10/12, 15/18, 20/24. (ii) 2/3: 4/6, 6/9, 8/12. (iii) 1/4: 2/8, 3/12, 4/16. (iv) 5/8: 10/16, 15/24, 20/32. (v) 3/5: 6/10, 9/15, 12/20. (vi) 2/5: 4/10, 6/15, 8/20.

lessons.title: Comparing Fractions With the Same Denominator
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

When two fractions have the same denominator, the fraction with the greater numerator is greater — the parts are the same size, so more parts means a bigger fraction.

Worked example: Put the correct symbol (>, < or =) (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: With the same denominator, compare the numerators.
Step: 5/8 < 7/8.
Step: 3/4 > 2/4.
Step: 1/3 < 2/3.
Step: 5/8 > 3/8.
Answer: 5/8 < 7/8; 3/4 > 2/4; 1/3 < 2/3; 5/8 > 3/8.

Worked example: Put the correct symbol (Exercise 4, Q2)

Step 1: With the same denominator, compare the numerators.
Step: 3/9 < 5/9.
Step: 3/5 > 2/5.
Step: 4/7 = 4/7.
Step: 2/3 > 1/3.
Step: 4/9 = 4/9.
Step: 5/11 > 3/11.
Answer: 3/9 < 5/9; 3/5 > 2/5; 4/7 = 4/7; 2/3 > 1/3; 4/9 = 4/9; 5/11 > 3/11.

The rule

lessons.title: Adding Lengths (m, cm and km)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Lengths are measured in centimetres (cm), metres (m) and kilometres (km): 1 m = 100 cm and 1 km = 1000 m. To add two lengths, add the smaller unit first, then the larger unit.

Worked example: Add the lengths (Exercise 1, Q1–Q6)

Step 1: Add the smaller unit first (cm with cm, m with m).
Step 2: Add the larger unit (m with m, km with km).
Step: (1) cm: 65 + 12 = 77; m: 4 + 5 = 9 — total 9 m 77 cm.
Step: (2) cm: 50 + 40 = 90; m: 14 + 9 = 23 — total 23 m 90 cm.
Step: (3) m: 632 + 214 = 846; km: 7 + 8 = 15 — total 15 km 846 m.
Step: (4) m: 312 + 676 = 988; km: 25 + 21 = 46 — total 46 km 988 m.
Step: (5) m: 815 + 183 = 998; km: 21 + 17 = 38 — total 38 km 998 m.
Step: (6) m: 745 + 134 = 879; km: 41 + 38 = 79 — total 79 km 879 m.
Answer: (1) 9 m 77 cm; (2) 23 m 90 cm; (3) 15 km 846 m; (4) 46 km 988 m; (5) 38 km 998 m; (6) 79 km 879 m.

lessons.title: Subtracting Capacities
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

To subtract two capacities, subtract the millilitres first, then the litres. If the millilitres are not enough, borrow 1 litre = 1000 ml.

Worked example: Subtract the capacities (Exercise 6, Q1)

Step 1: Subtract millilitres first, then litres, borrowing where needed.
Step: (i) ml: 655 − 321 = 334; l: 18 − 12 = 6 — 6 l 334 ml.
Step: (ii) ml: 742 − 421 = 321; l: 8 − 7 = 1 — 1 l 321 ml.
Step: (iii) ml: 758 − 0 = 758; l: 45 − 21 = 24 — 24 l 758 ml.
Step: (iv) ml: 450 − 300 = 150; l: 25 − 21 = 4 — 4 l 150 ml.
Step: (v) ml: 915 − 800 = 115; l: 75 − 61 = 14 — 14 l 115 ml.
Step: (vi) ml: 334 is less than 621, so borrow 1 litre (1000 ml): 1334 − 621 = 713; l: 57 − 35 = 22 — 22 l 713 ml.
Answer: (i) 6 l 334 ml; (ii) 1 l 321 ml; (iii) 24 l 758 ml; (iv) 4 l 150 ml; (v) 14 l 115 ml; (vi) 22 l 713 ml.

Worked example: A pot has 2000 ml of tea; 1500 ml is served (Exercise 6, Q2)

Step 1: Subtract: 2000 − 1500 = 500.
Answer: 500 ml of tea left.

Worked example: A container has 2 l 450 ml; 1 l 200 ml is drunk (Exercise 6, Q3)

Step 1: Subtract: 2 l 450 ml − 1 l 200 ml.
Step 2: ml: 450 − 200 = 250. l: 2 − 1 = 1.
Answer: 1 l 250 ml left.

Worked example: Subtract: 15 l 500 ml − 3 l (Exercise 6, Q4)

Step 1: Subtract litres: 15 − 3 = 12; the millilitres stay 500.
Answer: 12 l 500 ml.

lessons.title: Reading the Clock — a.m. and p.m.
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

The short hand of a clock shows the hour; the long hand shows the minutes. Each number on the clock face = 5 minutes, and each small mark = 1 minute. Times from midnight to noon are a.m.; times from noon to midnight are p.m.

Worked example: Write the time and a.m. or p.m. for each clock picture (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: Read the hour hand (short) and the minute hand (long).
Step 2: Morning times are a.m.; afternoon and evening times are p.m.
Step 3: (i) Morning picture: the clock shows 8:30 — a.m.
Step 4: (ii) Evening picture: 4:40 — p.m.
Step 5: (iii) School morning: 7:25 — a.m.
Step 6: (iv) Evening: 7:25 — p.m.
Step 7: (v) Dinner time: 8:35 — p.m.
Answer: (i) 8:30 a.m. (ii) 4:40 p.m. (iii) 7:25 a.m. (iv) 7:25 p.m. (v) 8:35 p.m.

Worked example: Read the time on each analogue clock (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: The short hand shows the hour; the long hand shows the minutes (each mark = 1 minute, each number = 5 minutes).
Step 2: Read the nine clocks one by one.
Answer: (i) 5:00; (ii) 6:40; (iii) 3:00; (iv) 4:05; (v) 5:40; (vi) 10:50; (vii) 8:55; (viii) 2:45; (ix) 1:30.

mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: the short hand of a clock shows the hour, and the long hand shows the minutes.

mcqs.q: What does the long hand of a clock show?
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: the long hand of a clock shows the minutes, and the short hand shows the hour.

mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: each number on the clock face = 5 minutes, and each small mark = 1 minute.

mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: each small mark = 1 minute, while each big number = 5 minutes.

mcqs.why: The short hand on 5 gives the hour 5, and the long hand on 12 gives 0 minutes, so the time is 5:00, as in the exercise.

lessons.title: Using a Calendar
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A calendar shows the days, weeks and months of a year. To answer a calendar question, find the month, then count the weeks and days from the 1st of that month. In the book's calendar, January 1 is a Friday.

Worked example: Use the calendar in the book (Exercise 2)

Step 1: (i) January has 31 days. January 1 is a Friday, so the Fridays are 1, 8, 15, 22, 29; January 31 is two days after Friday 29 — a Sunday.
Step 2: (ii) April 1 is a Thursday, so the Wednesdays of April are 7, 14, 21, 28; the second Wednesday is 14 April.
Step 3: (iii) December 1 is a Wednesday, so December 3 is a Friday.
Step 4: (iv) In February the Fridays are 5, 12, 19, 26; the last Friday is 26 February.
Step 5: (v) March 1 is a Monday, so the Tuesdays are 2, 9, 16, 23; 23rd March is a Tuesday.
Answer: (i) January 31 = Sunday. (ii) Second Wednesday of April = 14 April. (iii) 3rd December = Friday. (iv) Last Friday of February = 26 February. (v) 23rd March = Tuesday.

mcqs.q: How many days are there in January?
mcqs.why: The calendar work in the notes starts from this fact: January has 31 days, and its last day, January 31, is a Sunday.

mcqs.q: In the book's calendar, January 1 is a:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes states it directly: in the book's calendar, January 1 is a Friday.

mcqs.q: In the book's calendar, the Fridays of January are:
mcqs.why: January 1 is a Friday, and Fridays come every 7 days: 1 + 7 = 8, 8 + 7 = 15, 15 + 7 = 22 and 22 + 7 = 29.

mcqs.q: In the book's calendar, January 31 is a:
mcqs.why: The last Friday of January is the 29th, and January 31 is two days after Friday 29, which makes it a Sunday.

mcqs.why: April 1 is a Thursday, so the Wednesdays of April are 7, 14, 21, 28, and the second one is 14 April.

mcqs.why: December 1 is a Wednesday, so December 2 is a Thursday and December 3 is a Friday.

mcqs.q: In the book's calendar, the last Friday of February is:
mcqs.why: In February the Fridays are 5, 12, 19, 26, and the last of these dates is 26 February.

mcqs.q: In the book's calendar, 23rd March is a:
mcqs.why: March 1 is a Monday, so the Tuesdays of March are 2, 9, 16, 23, and 23rd March is a Tuesday.

mcqs.q: In the book's calendar, April 1 is a:
mcqs.why: The worked example in the notes begins: April 1 is a Thursday, so the Wednesdays of April are 7, 14, 21, 28.

mcqs.q: In the book's calendar, March 1 is a:
mcqs.why: The worked example in the notes begins: March 1 is a Monday, so the Tuesdays are 2, 9, 16, 23.

chapters.title: Unit 5: Measurement (Time) — Adding and Subtracting Hours

lessons.title: Adding Hours
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Hours add like ordinary numbers, because every hour is the same length: add the hour numbers and write the answer in hours.

Worked example: Add the hours (Exercise 3, Q1)

Step 1: Add each pair of hour numbers.
Step: (i) 5 + 3 = 8 hours.
Step: (ii) 6 + 4 = 10 hours.
Step: (iii) 10 + 5 = 15 hours.
Step: (iv) 10 + 8 = 18 hours.
Step: (v) 7 + 8 = 15 hours.
Step: (vi) 15 + 5 = 20 hours.
Answer: 5 + 3 = 8 hours; 6 + 4 = 10 hours; 10 + 5 = 15 hours; 10 + 8 = 18 hours; 7 + 8 = 15 hours; 15 + 5 = 20 hours.

Worked example: Add: 5 hours + 2 hours (Exercise 3)

Step 1: Add: 5 + 2 = 7.
Answer: 7 hours.

Worked example: Add: 10 hours + 8 hours (Exercise 3)

Step 1: Add: 10 + 8 = 18.
Answer: 18 hours.

Worked example: Add: 9 hours + 8 hours (Exercise 3)

Step 1: Add: 9 + 8 = 17.
Answer: 17 hours.

lessons.title: Subtracting Hours
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

To find how much longer or shorter one time is than another, subtract the smaller number of hours from the bigger one.

Worked example: Subtract the hours (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: Subtract each pair of hour numbers.
Step: (i) 8 − 5 = 3 hours.
Step: (ii) 18 − 7 = 11 hours.
Step: (iii) 15 − 6 = 9 hours.
Step: (iv) 18 − 11 = 7 hours.
Step: (v) 16 − 10 = 6 hours.
Step: (vi) 21 − 8 = 13 hours.
Answer: 8 − 5 = 3 hours; 18 − 7 = 11 hours; 15 − 6 = 9 hours; 18 − 11 = 7 hours; 16 − 10 = 6 hours; 21 − 8 = 13 hours.

Worked example: Areesha starts work at 11:00 a.m. and works for 2 hours (Exercise 4, Q2)

Step 1: (a) How many more hours is 4 hours than 2 hours? Subtract: 4 − 2 = 2 more hours.
Step 2: (b) Add the working time to the starting time: 11:00 a.m. + 2 hours = 1:00 p.m.
Answer: (a) 2 more hours. (b) She stops at 1:00 p.m.

Worked example: Subtract: 8 hours − 5 hours (Exercise 4, Q3)

Step 1: Subtract: 8 − 5 = 3.
Answer: 3 hours.

Worked example: 8 hours and 5 hours: how many hours less is the smaller time? (Exercise 4, Q4)

Step 1: Subtract: 8 − 5 = 3.
Step 2: The book's question is about the time for Mathematics, which is the smaller time.
Answer: 3 hours less for Mathematics.

mcqs.why: Subtract the smaller number of hours from the bigger one: 8 - 5 = 3, giving 3 hours.

mcqs.why: To compare the two times, subtract: 4 - 2 = 2, so 4 hours is 2 more hours than 2 hours.

mcqs.why: Add the working time to the starting time: 11 + 2 = 13, and the 13th hour of the day is 1:00 p.m., so she stops at 1:00 p.m.

mcqs.why: Subtract the smaller time from the bigger time: 8 - 5 = 3, so Mathematics gets 3 hours less, as the book's question asks.

chapters.title: Unit 6: Geometry — Points, Lines and Perimeter

lessons.title: Point, Line, Line Segment and Ray
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A point is a single dot — it shows an exact position. A line segment joins two end points and stops there. A ray starts at one end point and goes on forever through an arrow at the other end. A line has arrows at both ends and goes on forever both ways.

Worked example: Identify each figure (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: A figure with two end points is a line segment.
Step 2: A figure with one end point and one arrow is a ray.
Step 3: A figure with arrows at both ends is a line.
Step 4: A single dot is a point.
Step: AB (dots at both ends) = line segment.
Step: CD (dot at C, arrow at D) = ray.
Step: X (a single dot) = point.
Step: EF (arrows at both ends) = line.
Step: YX (arrow at Y, dot at X) = ray.
Step: PQ (dots at both ends) = line segment.
Answer: AB = line segment; CD = ray; X = point; EF = line; YX = ray; PQ = line segment.

Measuring line segments (Exercise 1, Q2)

Place the ruler's 0 mark at one end of the segment and read the mark at the other end in centimetres and millimetres. Measured from the PDF page scale, the segments are: AB = 8.3 cm (83 mm); CD = 6.7 cm (67 mm); EF = 10.2 cm (102 mm). Note: these ruler readings were measured from the PDF page scale — if the book is printed at a different size, the readings on the printed page may differ slightly (activity-based readings).

Worked example: Draw line segments of (i) 1.9 cm, (ii) 4.2 cm, (iii) 5.6 cm (Exercise 1, Q3)

Step 1: Mark the starting point at 0 on the ruler.
Step 2: Mark the end point at the given length.
Step 3: Join the two points with a straight line and label the ends.
Answer: (i) A segment 1.9 cm long. (ii) A segment 4.2 cm long. (iii) A segment 5.6 cm long.

Worked example: Identify each figure (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: Two end points means line segment; one end point and one arrow means ray; arrows at both ends means line; a single dot means point.
Step: AB = line segment.
Step: Y = point.
Step: EF = ray.
Step: CD = line segment.
Step: PQ = line.
Step: RS = ray.
Step: X = point.
Step: MN = line.
Step: JK = line segment.
Answer: AB = line segment; Y = point; EF = ray; CD = line segment; PQ = line; RS = ray; X = point; MN = line; JK = line segment. (MN has arrows at both ends, so it is a line, not a ray.)

mcqs.q: A single dot that shows an exact position is called a:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: a point is a single dot, and it shows an exact position.

mcqs.q: A figure that joins two end points and stops there is a:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: a line segment joins two end points and stops there, while a ray goes on forever from one end point.

mcqs.q: A figure that starts at one end point and goes on forever through an arrow is a:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: a ray starts at one end point and goes on forever through an arrow at the other end.

mcqs.q: A figure with arrows at both ends, going on forever both ways, is a:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: a line has arrows at both ends and goes on forever in both directions.

mcqs.q: In the exercise, YX has an arrow at Y and a dot at X. YX is a:
mcqs.why: YX has one end point (the dot at X) and one arrow (at Y), and a figure with one end point and one arrow is a ray.

mcqs.q: In the exercise, MN has arrows at both ends. MN is a:
mcqs.why: The notes point this out specially: MN has arrows at both ends, so it is a line, not a ray.

mcqs.q: Measured from the page, the segment AB in the measuring activity is:
mcqs.why: The notes give the ruler readings from the page scale: AB = 8.3 cm (83 mm), CD = 6.7 cm and EF = 10.2 cm.

mcqs.q: To draw a line segment of 1.9 cm, the end point is marked at:
mcqs.why: The steps in the notes: mark the starting point at 0 on the ruler, mark the end point at the given length, 1.9 cm, then join the two points.

mcqs.q: Measured from the page, the segment CD in the measuring activity is:
mcqs.why: The notes give the ruler readings from the page scale: CD = 6.7 cm (67 mm), AB = 8.3 cm and EF = 10.2 cm.

mcqs.q: A ray goes on forever:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: a ray starts at one end point and goes on forever in that one direction; a line is the one that goes on both ways.

lessons.title: Perimeter of Squares, Rectangles and Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

The perimeter of a closed figure is the sum of the lengths of all its sides. Perimeter of a square = 4 x side. Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 x (length + width). Perimeter of a triangle = side + side + side.

Worked example: Measure each side and find the perimeter (Exercise 2, Q2)

Step 1: Measure each side with a ruler (measured from the PDF page scale — on a differently printed page the readings may differ slightly).
Step 2: (i) Square ABCD: AB = BC = CD = AD = 4 cm. Perimeter = 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 cm.
Step 3: (ii) Rectangle PQRS: PQ = 6.2 cm, QR = 3.5 cm, RS = 6.2 cm, PS = 3.5 cm. Perimeter = 6.2 + 3.5 + 6.2 + 3.5 = 19.4 cm.
Step 4: (iii) Triangle XYZ: XY = 4.6 cm, YZ = 4.6 cm, XZ = 4.6 cm. Perimeter = 4.6 + 4.6 + 4.6 = 13.8 cm.
Answer: (i) 16 cm. (ii) 19.4 cm. (iii) 13.8 cm.

Worked example: Perimeter of a square of side (i) 3 cm, (ii) 4 cm (Exercise 2, Q3)

Step 1: Perimeter of a square = 4 x side.
Step 2: (i) 4 x 3 = 12 cm.
Step 3: (ii) 4 x 4 = 16 cm.
Answer: (i) 12 cm. (ii) 16 cm.

Worked example: Perimeter of the rectangles: (i) 4 cm by 5 cm, (ii) 4 cm by 6 cm (Exercise 2, Q4)

Step 1: Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 x (length + width).
Step 2: (i) 2 x (4 + 5) = 2 x 9 = 18 cm.
Step 3: (ii) 2 x (4 + 6) = 2 x 10 = 20 cm.
Answer: (i) 18 cm. (ii) 20 cm.

Worked example: Perimeter of the triangles: (i) sides 4 cm, 5 cm, 3 cm, (ii) sides 4 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm (Exercise 2, Q5)

Step 1: Perimeter of a triangle = sum of its three sides.
Step 2: (i) 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 cm.
Step 3: (ii) 4 + 4 + 5 = 13 cm.
Answer: (i) 12 cm. (ii) 13 cm.

mcqs.q: The perimeter of a square is found by:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: the perimeter of a square = 4 x side, because all four sides of a square are equal.

mcqs.q: What is the perimeter of a square of side 3 cm?
mcqs.why: Use the square rule: perimeter = 4 x 3 = 12, so the perimeter is 12 cm.

mcqs.q: What is the perimeter of a square of side 4 cm?
mcqs.why: Use the square rule: perimeter = 4 x 4 = 16, so the perimeter is 16 cm.

mcqs.q: What is the perimeter of a rectangle 4 cm long and 5 cm wide?
mcqs.why: Use the rectangle rule: first add the length and width, 4 + 5 = 9, then double the result: 2 x 9 = 18, so the perimeter is 18 cm.

mcqs.q: What is the perimeter of a rectangle 4 cm long and 6 cm wide?
mcqs.why: Use the rectangle rule: first add the length and width, 4 + 6 = 10, then double the result: 2 x 10 = 20, so the perimeter is 20 cm.

mcqs.q: What is the perimeter of a triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm?
mcqs.why: The perimeter of a triangle is the sum of its three sides: 4 + 5 + 3 = 12, so the perimeter is 12 cm.

mcqs.q: What is the perimeter of a triangle with sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm?
mcqs.why: The perimeter of a triangle is the sum of its three sides: 4 + 4 + 5 = 13, so the perimeter is 13 cm.

mcqs.q: The perimeter of a closed figure is:
options: The sum of the lengths of all its sides
The length of its longest side only
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: the perimeter of a closed figure is the sum of the lengths of all its sides.

mcqs.q: A rectangle has sides 6.2 cm, 3.5 cm, 6.2 cm and 3.5 cm. Its perimeter is:
mcqs.why: Add all four sides: 6.2 + 3.5 + 6.2 + 3.5 = 19.4, so the perimeter of rectangle PQRS is 19.4 cm.

mcqs.q: A triangle has all three sides equal to 4.6 cm. Its perimeter is:
mcqs.why: Add the three equal sides: 4.6 + 4.6 + 4.6 = 13.8, so the perimeter of triangle XYZ is 13.8 cm.

chapters.title: Unit 6: Geometry — Circles, Symmetry and 3-D Shapes

lessons.title: The Circle — Centre, Radius and Diameter
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

The middle point of a circle is its centre. A line from the centre to the edge (circumference) is a radius. A line from one side of the circle to the other, passing through the centre, is a diameter.

Worked example: Identify the parts of the circle (Exercise 2, Q6)

Step 1: The dot A in the middle is the centre.
Step 2: The line from O to A (centre to circumference) is a radius.
Step 3: The line from B to C (circumference to centre) is also a radius.
Step 4: The line from C to D passing through O (end to end through the centre) is the diameter.
Answer: (i) Centre; (ii) Radius; (iii) Radius; (iv) Diameter.

mcqs.q: The middle point of a circle is called its:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: the middle point of a circle is its centre, like the dot A in the middle in the exercise.

mcqs.q: A line from the centre of a circle to its edge is called a:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: a line from the centre to the edge (circumference) is a radius.

mcqs.q: A line from one side of a circle to the other, passing through the centre, is called a:
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: a line from one side of the circle to the other, passing through the centre, is a diameter.

mcqs.q: The edge of a circle is called its:
mcqs.why: The notes name the edge of the circle when defining the radius: the line goes from the centre to the edge, the circumference.

lessons.title: Lines of Symmetry
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A line of symmetry divides a figure into two halves that match exactly when folded on that line. A figure may have 0, 1, 2 or more lines of symmetry.

Worked example: How many lines of symmetry does each figure have? (Exercise 3, Q1)

Step 1: Fold the figure mentally along each possible line and check whether the two halves match.
Step 2: (i) Half-rounded rectangle: 1 horizontal line.
Step 3: (ii) Square: 4 lines.
Step 4: (iii) Letter A: 1 vertical line.
Step 5: (iv) Tall isosceles triangle: 1 vertical line (the triangle is taller than it is wide, so it is not equilateral).
Step 6: (v) Elongated hexagon: 2 lines (horizontal and vertical).
Step 7: (vi) Kite: 1 vertical line.
Answer: (i) 1; (ii) 4; (iii) 1; (iv) 1; (v) 2; (vi) 1.

Worked example: How many lines of symmetry are shown by the dashed lines? (Exercise 3, Q2)

Step 1: Count the dashed lines drawn on each figure.
Answer: (i) Circle: 2. (ii) Rhombus: 2. (iii) Flower: 1. (iv) Plus-shape: 4. (v) Letter H: 2. (vi) Pentagon: 5.

mcqs.q: A line of symmetry divides a figure into:
options: Two halves that are always different
Two halves that match exactly when folded
mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: a line of symmetry divides a figure into two halves that match exactly when folded on that line.

lessons.title: Sorting With Carroll Diagrams
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A Carroll diagram sorts things by two questions at the same time. Every item goes into exactly one box: check the first question (for example even or odd), then the second question (for example divisible by 5 or not).

Worked example: Carroll panel from the teaching pages (book page 162)

Step 1: Check each number for even/odd and for divisibility by 5 (a number is divisible by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5).
Step 2: Even and divisible by 5: 10, 20, 30.
Step 3: Odd and divisible by 5: 5, 15, 25.
Step 4: Even and not divisible by 5: 4, 8, 14.
Step 5: Odd and not divisible by 5: 3, 9, 19, 21.
Answer: (i) Smallest even number divisible by 5 = 10 (given in the book). (ii) Odd numbers divisible by 5: 5, 15, 25. (iii) Smallest even number not divisible by 5 = 4. (iv) Greatest odd number not divisible by 5 = 21.

Fruits and vegetables (Exercise 1, Q1)

Sort the pictured fruits and vegetables into the two groups of the Carroll diagram. Fruits: mango, plum, peach, pear, cherry, watermelon, apple (7). Vegetables: bitter gourd, capsicum, eggplant, carrot, green chilli, tomato (6). Tomato is placed with the vegetables, following the usual school convention; botanically it is a fruit, but in everyday cooking it is treated as a vegetable.

Worked example: Sort (10, 18, 22, 25, 29, 30, 35, 37, 45, 43, 48, 52) into a Carroll diagram (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: Check each number for even/odd.
Step 2: Check divisibility by 5 (ends in 0 or 5).
Answer: Even and divisible by 5: 10, 30. Odd and divisible by 5: 25, 35, 45. Even and not divisible by 5: 18, 22, 48, 52. Odd and not divisible by 5: 29, 37, 43.

Worked example: Carroll diagram: less than 25 / greater than 25 and divisible by 7 / not (Exercise 1, Q3)

Step 1: Compare each number with 25.
Step 2: Check divisibility by 7.
Answer: (i) Greater and divisible by 7: 28, 35, 42. (ii) Greater and not divisible by 7: 27, 29, 38, 43. (iii) Less and divisible by 7: 7, 14, 21. (iv) Less and not divisible by 7: 5, 9, 15, 19.

lessons.title: Tally Charts
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A tally chart counts things with tally marks — one mark for each item, grouped in fives. To read a tally chart, count the marks in each row.

Worked example: Tally panel: animals seen (teaching pages, book pages 162–163)

Step 1: Read each tally count: Monkey 7, Lion 6, Bear 4, Zebra 6, Elephant 2.
Step 2: Least = Elephant (given in the book). Greatest = Monkey (7).
Step 3: Equal counts: Lion and Zebra (6 each).
Step 4: Monkey + Lion = 7 + 6 = 13.
Step 5: Total = 7 + 6 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 25.
Answer: Least: Elephant. Greatest: Monkey (7). Equal: Lion and Zebra. Monkey + Lion = 13. Total = 25.

Worked example: A die is rolled 20 times — make a tally chart (Exercise 1, Q4)

Step 1: Count how many times each number from 1 to 6 appears in: 1, 3, 5, 6, 3, 2, 4, 5, 3, 2, 4, 6, 3, 4, 3, 4, 2, 5, 1, 6.
Step 2: Check the counts add up to 20.
Answer: 1: 2 times; 2: 3 times; 3: 5 times; 4: 4 times; 5: 3 times; 6: 3 times. Total = 20.

Worked example: Birthday tally: January 3, February 6, March 10, April 7, May 4 (Exercise 1, Q5)

Step 1: Compare the counts.
Step 2: Least = January (3). Greatest = March (10).
Step 3: January + April = 3 + 7 = 10.
Step 4: Total = 3 + 6 + 10 + 7 + 4 = 30.
Answer: (i) Least = January (3). (ii) Greatest = March (10). (iii) January + April = 10. (iv) Total = 30.

mcqs.why: The counts are Monkey 7, Lion 6, Bear 4, Zebra 6 and Elephant 2, so the lion and the zebra are equal at 6 each.

mcqs.why: Add the two tally counts: 7 + 6 = 13, so monkeys and lions together make 13.

mcqs.why: Add all the tally counts: 7 + 6 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 25, so 25 animals were seen in total.

lessons.title: Pictographs
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A pictograph shows numbers with pictures. Always read the key first: the key tells what 1 picture stands for. Multiply the number of pictures by the key value to find the real number.

Worked example: Sports pictograph panel (book page 166; 1 picture = 2 students)

Step 1: Multiply the number of pictures by 2.
Step: Hockey: 5 pictures x 2 = 10 students.
Step: Football: 6 pictures x 2 = 12 students.
Step: Cricket: 4 pictures x 2 = 8 students.
Step: Tennis: 3 pictures x 2 = 6 students.
Step: Table Tennis: 2 pictures x 2 = 4 students.
Answer: Hockey = 10; Football = 12; Cricket = 8; Tennis = 6; Table Tennis = 4. Most = Football (12). Least = Table Tennis (4).

Worked example: Pictograph of students present (1 picture = 1 student) (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: With the key 1 picture = 1 student, count the pictures for each day.
Answer: (i) Monday = 4. (ii) Tuesday = 3. (iii) Most = Thursday (6). (iv) Least = Friday (2). (v) Wednesday + Thursday = 5 + 6 = 11.

Worked example: Pictograph of cars sold (1 picture = 100 cars) (Exercise 2, Q2)

Step 1: Multiply the number of pictures by 100.
Step: 2008: 4 pictures x 100 = 400 cars.
Step: 2009: 5 pictures x 100 = 500 cars.
Step: 2010: 3 pictures x 100 = 300 cars.
Step: 2011: 4 pictures x 100 = 400 cars.
Step: 2012: 2 pictures x 100 = 200 cars.
Answer: 2008 = 400; 2009 = 500; 2010 = 300; 2011 = 400; 2012 = 200. (i) 2008 = 400. (ii) 2010 = 300. (iii) Most = 2009 (500). (iv) Least = 2012 (200). (v) Equal = 2008 and 2011 (400 each).

mcqs.why: The rule in the notes: a pictograph shows numbers with pictures, and we must always read the key first, because it tells what 1 picture stands for.

mcqs.why: Table Tennis has only 2 pictures, and 2 x 2 = 4 students, which is the smallest count in the pictograph.

mcqs.why: Both 2008 and 2011 have 4 pictures, and 4 x 100 = 400 cars each, so their sales are equal.
